controls_catalog.description: Controles derivados del 'Securing Agentic Applications Guide 1.0', organizados por dominio. Cada control incluye su área, descripción y las amenazas (T-IDs) que mitiga.

controls.name: OAuth 2.0/OIDC with Least Privilege Scopes
controls.description: Implement OAuth 2.0 for permissions and authorization. Use authorization code flow with PKCE. Grant only minimum necessary permissions. Grant agents short-lived access tokens.

controls.name: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) with Granular Roles
controls.description: Define granular roles specific to agent functions. Implement permission matrices to track role capabilities. Distinguish between read and write access; default to read-only.

controls.name: Just-in-Time (JIT) Credential Issuance
controls.description: Implement temporary credentials with a limited scope and lifetime. Generate credentials only when needed and ensure they expire quickly.

controls.name: Managed Identity Services (no hardcoded credentials)
controls.description: Configure cloud providers' identity services instead of embedding credentials. Use AWS IAM roles or Azure Managed Identities.

controls.name: Separation of Control Planes in Multi-Agent Systems
controls.description: Create a clear separation between different agent functionalities. Maintain distinct permission sets for each agent based on least privilege.

controls.name: Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and Verifiable Credentials (VCs)
controls.description: Use W3C standard DIDs for self-sovereign agent identities. Implement VCs for agents to prove specific attributes. Enable verification without a central authority.

controls.name: Encryption at Rest and in Transit
controls.description: Use strong encryption algorithms for data at rest and in transit. Implement TLS 1.2+ for transit, AES-256-GCM for storage.

controls.name: Data Loss Prevention (DLP)
controls.description: Deploy DLP solutions to monitor and prevent leakage of sensitive information. Set up scanning of data inputs/outputs to detect PII, credentials, or other sensitive data.

controls.name: Data Classification and Sensitivity Labels
controls.description: Apply labels that guide the AI agent's access and handling of data before being accessed. Create tiered classifications like public, internal, confidential, and restricted.

controls.name: Memory Segmentation and Session Isolation
controls.description: Isolate user sessions and domain contexts to prevent knowledge and sensitive data leakage. Wipe state between tasks. Use per-tenant namespaces in shared vector stores.

controls.name: Memory TTL and Expiration
controls.description: Expire old or stale memory content automatically. Expire unverified memory to limit poison persistence. Decay low-trust entries over time.

controls.name: PII Detection and Redaction before Memory Storage
controls.description: Implement robust PII detection and removal/masking before memory storage. Use regex (for structured PII), NER models, dedicated services (Microsoft Presidio SDK).

controls.name: Input Validation and Sanitization
controls.description: Filter user inputs using rule-based patterns and NLP techniques. Check for malicious patterns before processing. Escape or strip special tokens (##, <<, {{}}) before injecting user input into prompts.

controls.name: System Prompt Hardening
controls.description: Embed security policies directly into the AI's foundational instructions. Explicitly state DOs and DON'Ts, forbidden topics, operational scope. Use clear delimiters to separate instructions from user input.

controls.name: Output Filtering and Content Moderation
controls.description: Screen AI-generated responses for inappropriate or harmful content. Use both pattern matching and ML-based content classifiers. Apply AI guardrails to both inputs and outputs.

controls.name: Schema Enforcement on Tool Arguments and Outputs
controls.description: Define strict schemas for tool arguments and expected outputs. Use structured formats like JSON to constrain output to a predictable schema. Fail closed on ambiguous resolution.

controls.name: Allow/Deny Lists for Tool Arguments and Content
controls.description: Use allow lists for known-good values and deny lists for known-bad patterns in tool arguments or outputs. Enforce fully qualified tool names and version pins to avoid tool alias collisions.

controls.name: Secure Rendering of Agent Output in UIs
controls.description: Use safe methods for displaying agent output (e.g., element.textContent instead of element.innerHTML). Implement CSP HTTP headers. Use DOMPurify or sanitize-html libraries.

controls.name: Least Privilege per Tool (Fine-Grained OAuth Scopes or API Keys)
controls.description: Define per-tool least-privilege profiles (scopes, maximum rate, and egress allowlists). Enforce least agency: read-only queries for databases, no send/delete rights for email summarizers.

controls.name: Mandatory Sandboxing for Tool and Code Execution
controls.description: Run tool or code execution in isolated sandboxes (OS-level isolation, containers, VMs, WebAssembly). Set strict CPU, memory, and execution time limits. Automatically reset sandbox after each tool execution.

controls.name: Allow/Deny Lists for APIs and Network Destinations
controls.description: Prevent manipulation via prompt injection or compromised tools. Configure a list of permitted base URLs (Allow-List). Use an outward proxy or API Gateway to permit connections only to pre-approved destinations.

controls.name: Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) for High-Impact Tool Actions
controls.description: Require explicit user consent and human confirmation for high-impact or destructive actions (delete, transfer, publish). Display a pre-execution plan or dry-run diff before final approval.

controls.name: Rate Limiting and Adaptive Tool Budgeting
controls.description: Apply usage ceilings (cost, rate, or token budgets) with automatic revocation or throttling when exceeded. Implement AI rate-limiting policies to restrict high-frequency task requests per agent session.

controls.name: Static Analysis on Agent-Generated Code
controls.description: Use tools like Bandit (Python), Semgrep (multi-language), CodeShield (LLM-generated code). Do static scans before execution. Require human approval for elevated runs.

controls.name: Parameterized Queries and ORM for Database Access
controls.description: Use parameterized or template queries/ORMs exclusively. Never construct SQL using string concatenation. Filter/block dangerous SQL keywords (e.g., DROP, TRUNCATE). Grant database access via least-privilege user accounts.

controls.name: URL Security and Web Browsing Controls
controls.description: Use URL filtering with allow lists. Leverage Secure Web Gateway (SWG) or Data Loss Prevention (DLP). Perform reputation checks on target domains. Enforce proper TLS verification. Implement content sanitization before processing.

controls.name: Mutual TLS (mTLS) for Inter-Agent Communication
controls.description: Use protocols with strong encryption for all agent interactions. Implement mutual TLS (mTLS) for two-way authentication. Sign and verify all inter-agent messages.

controls.name: Policy Enforcement Points (PEPs) on Communication Channels
controls.description: Add security checkpoints to communication channels for policy enforcement. Implement as middleware or service proxies that validate each interaction.

controls.name: Zero Trust Architecture for Agent-to-Agent Trust
controls.description: Implement a 'never trust, always verify' approach across the architecture. Verify every access request regardless of source. Apply Zero Trust principles per NIST SP 800-207.

controls.name: Anti-Replay Protection (Nonces, Session IDs, Timestamps)
controls.description: Protect all exchanges with nonces, session identifiers, and timestamps tied to task windows. Maintain short-term message fingerprints or state hashes to detect cross-context replays.

controls.name: Typed Message Schemas with Version Enforcement
controls.description: Use versioned, typed message schemas with explicit per-message audiences. Reject messages that fail validation or attempt schema down-conversion. Disable weak or legacy communication modes.

controls.name: Attested Agent Registry and Cryptographic Agent Identity
controls.description: Use registries that provide digital attestation of agent identity, provenance, and descriptor integrity. Require signed agent cards. No open registration. Leverage PKI trusted root certificate registries.

source_sections: 6 Agentic AI and the Supply Chain

controls.name: SBOMs, AIBOMs, and Agent SBOMs with Attestation
controls.description: Sign and attest manifests, prompts, and tool definitions. Require and operationalize SBOMs, AIBOMs with periodic attestations. Maintain inventory of AI components.

controls.name: Dependency Allowlisting and Pinning by Content Hash
controls.description: Allowlist and pin dependencies. Scan for typosquats (PyPI, npm, LangChain, LlamaIndex). Verify provenance before install or activation. Auto-reject unsigned or unverified components.

controls.name: Version Control for Prompts, Tools, and Orchestration Scripts
controls.description: Put prompts, orchestration scripts, and memory schemas under version control with peer review. Scan for anomalies. Require staged rollout with differential tests and auto-rollback on hash drift.

controls.name: Supply Chain Kill Switch
controls.description: Implement emergency revocation mechanisms that can instantly disable specific tools, prompts, or agent connections across all deployments when a compromise is detected.

controls.name: Immutable Logs of All Agent Actions (Tool Calls, Memory Writes, Plans)
controls.description: Record comprehensive logs of all agent activities. Every agent action (tool use, messages, memory write) should be logged with timestamp, agentID, sessionID, payload hash. Store with forward integrity (append-only + Merkle proofs or signed logs).

controls.name: Behavioral Baseline and Anomaly Detection
controls.description: Establish behavioral patterns to detect anomalies. Use ML to detect unusual behavior patterns (ML-enabled SIEM). Detect fast-spreading commands and throttle or pause on anomalies. Monitor for unusual tool invocation patterns, cross-agent communication deviations.

controls.name: Tool Invocation Monitoring with Rate Limiting per Session
controls.description: Log all tool calls, parameters, and results. Monitor unusual frequency, suspicious parameter values, or calls to sensitive tools. Implement rate limiting per session/user and timeouts.

controls.name: Kill Switches and Emergency Agent Disablement
controls.description: Implement kill switches to immediately revoke access privileges. Create automated and manual mechanisms to stop agent operations. Implement rapid credential revocation to instantly disable rogue agents.

controls.name: Incident Response Plan for AI Agent Security Incidents
controls.description: Define what constitutes an incident (successful prompt injection causing harm, data breach via agent, agent performing unauthorized actions). Outline steps for containment, analysis, remediation, and reporting. Regularly test the plan.

controls.name: SIEM Integration and Centralized Observability
controls.description: Feed logs and alerts into a Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system for centralized analysis. Use MLFlow, Langfuse, LangSmith, Cloud provider tools. Implement trace IDs that propagate through agent steps.

controls.name: Role Containerization or Function-as-a-Service (FaaS)
controls.description: Each agent or distinct agent role should operate within a strongly isolated environment. Utilize containerization (Docker with Kubernetes) or FaaS (AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions) with strict resource limits and ephemeral execution contexts.

controls.name: API/Agent Gateway for All Tool Invocations
controls.description: An API/Agent Gateway should mediate all tool invocations, enforcing strict authentication and authorization. Implement granular rate limiting per agent or per tool. The gateway serves as a vital point for logging and auditing all tool interactions.

controls.name: Secure CI/CD with Vulnerability Scanning for Agent Logic
controls.description: Implementing rigorous CI/CD pipelines incorporating automated vulnerability scanning of dependencies, static analysis focusing on potential insecure Agent tool usage patterns, and dynamic testing specifically designed to probe for prompt injection vulnerabilities.

controls.name: Managing Non-Human Identities with Lifecycle Controls
controls.description: Each agent instance requires a distinct, manageable identity. Machine identities (service accounts, workload identities) must be treated with the same rigor as human identities, including secure provisioning, credential management, and reliable de-provisioning.

controls.name: Human Oversight in High-Stakes Environments
controls.description: Where critical decisions or high-risk actions require explicit human review, implement robust human-in-the-loop workflow. For agents in finance, healthcare, education, or critical infrastructure, consider Human-Over-The-Loop (continuous supervision). Adaptive trust mechanisms can dynamically adjust level of oversight.

controls.name: Behavioral Anomaly Alerting and Real-Time Override
controls.description: Systems should baseline normal agent behavior and trigger alerts upon significant deviations. Particular attention to unexpected or unauthorized tool use attempts, sudden shifts in the agent's apparent goal, or anomalous patterns in data access.

assurance_methods.description: Métodos de aseguramiento derivados de la Sección 7 de 'Securing Agentic Applications Guide 1.0'. Definen cómo probar que los controles funcionan.

methods.name: Red Teaming Agentic Applications
methods.description: Red teaming simulates adversarial attacks to detect and address vulnerabilities. Strategy requires assessing complex interactions, autonomous decision-making, and integration with external systems. Proactive red teaming identifies possible attack vectors including not only prompt injection techniques, but also privilege escalation through tools, memory poisoning, and plan manipulation.
scope_areas: Prompt injection attacks and red teaming detection strategies
Privilege escalation through tools and inter-agent relationships

tools.name: AgentDojo
tools.description: A dynamic evaluation framework to evaluate prompt injection attacks and defenses for LLM agents. Contains targeted injection attacks, instructing the agent to execute malicious tasks using available tools.

tools.name: Agentic Radar
tools.description: Designed to analyze and assess agentic systems for security and operational insights. Helps identify potential vulnerabilities in how agentic systems function.

tools.name: Agent-SafetyBench
tools.description: An evaluation benchmark to assess the safety of LLM agents. Comprises prompts or situations designed to evaluate whether agents follow safety norms and prevent creating damaging, unethical, or risky content or actions.

tools.name: AgentFence
tools.description: Red team tool equipped with multiple attack scenarios focusing on identifying vulnerabilities like prompt injection, role confusion, and system instruction leakage.

tools.name: Agent Security Bench (ASB)
tools.description: Red team tool with attack scenarios including Direct Prompt Injections (DPI), Indirect Prompt Injections (IPI), Plan-of-Thought (PoT) Backdoor, and Memory Poisoning Attacks.

tools.name: AgentPoison
tools.description: Red teaming tool used for injecting malicious instances into the knowledge base or memory, to be retrieved when specific triggers appear in the input query.

tools.name: MAPS (Multilingual Benchmark for Agent Security)
tools.description: Security evaluation benchmark assessing multi-lingual security of AI agents based on multi-lingual adaptation of well known agentic benchmarks translated to 10 different languages.

methods.name: Behavioral Testing for Agentic Applications
methods.description: Behavioral testing emphasizes evaluating agent activities and interactions rather than solely examining underlying structure or code. Aims to uncover unexpected actions, logical errors, or the pursuit of harmful goals. Methods require defining explicit objectives for the agent, utilizing benchmark datasets, executing simulations in regulated environments, and employing both human and automated assessments.

evaluation_frameworks.name: Inspect_evals (UK AI Safety Institute)
evaluation_frameworks.description: Open source framework to evaluate any generative model on any benchmark.

evaluation_frameworks.name: GenAI evaluation service (Google)
evaluation_frameworks.description: Evaluation framework for any generative model or application and benchmark the evaluation results against defined judgment.

evaluation_frameworks.name: Bedrock Evaluations (Amazon)
evaluation_frameworks.description: Evaluation framework for LLMs and integration with external sources as RAGs.

benchmark_selection_steps: Define Security Objectives: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability, Adversarial Robustness, Privacy Protection, Transparency and Accountability, Governance and Compliance.
Assess Threat Landscape: Data poisoning, adversarial attacks, model extraction, privacy breaches, DoS, misuse of agent autonomy.
Research Existing Benchmarks addressing agentic AI vulnerabilities.
Evaluate Benchmark Criteria: Align with security objectives, cover relevant threats, are standardized and widely accepted, provide actionable insights.
Test Benchmark Suitability focusing on false positives, effectiveness under adversarial conditions, resilience under attack.
Establish Continuous Evaluation: Regularly re-test with updated benchmarks. Integrate benchmarks into CI/CD pipelines.
Engage with the AI Security Community.

methods.name: Explainability Audits
methods.description: Use CoT for some insight into agentic reasoning, understanding that what the agent says and 'thinks' aren't necessarily aligned. Utilize HITL at critical junctions to understand and gate agent actions. Record agent-to-agent goal negotiations and tool interactions to understand additional inputs that may be misdirecting an agent.
techniques: Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning traces for agentic reasoning insight
HITL at critical junctions to gate agent actions (criticality defined by EU AI Act)
Explainable AI (XAI) strategies: SHAP, LIME, Grad-CAM, or T-SNE
Record agent-to-agent goal negotiations and tool interactions
Log which permission sets or identities were used for agentic actions

methods.name: Continuous Monitoring & Anomaly Detection (Runtime)
methods.description: Runtime observability must capture decisions, plan evolution, memory access patterns, and agent-tool interactions. Behavioral drift must trigger alerts or invoke safeguards. Agents should log timestamped reasoning traces for post-incident analysis.
techniques: LLM Input/Output Scanning: Monitor prompts and responses for jailbreak techniques, policy violations, PII.
Tool Invocation Monitoring: Log all tool calls, parameters, and results. Monitor unusual frequency or suspicious parameter values.
Plan & Execution Monitoring: Pre-execution checks and runtime monitoring of code execution within sandboxes.
Memory Anomaly Detection: Monitor memory update patterns for unusual frequency, size, or content.
Behavioral Analysis (Multi-Agent): Monitor communication patterns between agents for collusion, manipulation, or unexpected emergent behavior.
SIEM Integration for centralized analysis and correlation.
Automated Anomaly Response: Compute quarantine, circuit breakers, automated scaling, or credential revocation.

methods.name: Vulnerability Scanning (Runtime)
methods.description: Continuously scan the running application and environment for new vulnerabilities.
techniques: DAST scanning against lower environments for APIs and common interfaces (OWASP ZAP).
Port and CVE scanners for environment endpoints.
Integrate findings into a patch management process.

playbooks.description: 6 playbooks del documento 'Agentic AI – Threats and Mitigations v1.1'. Cada playbook es una guía operativa con 3 pasos: Step 1 Proactivo, Step 2 Reactivo y Step 3 Detective, para mitigar amenazas específicas.

items.name: Playbook 1: Preventing AI Agent Reasoning Manipulation
items.goal: Prevent attackers from manipulating AI intent, security bypasses through deceptive AI behaviors, and enhance AI actions traceability.

steps.label: Reduce attack surface & Implement Agent behavior profiling
actions: Restrict tool access to minimize the attack surface and prevent manipulation of user interactions.
Implement validation mechanisms to detect and filter manipulated responses in AI outputs.
Implement monitoring capabilities to ensure AI agent behavior aligns with its defined role and expected actions, preventing manipulation attempts.

steps.label: Prevent AI agent Goal Manipulation
actions: Use goal consistency validation to detect and block unintended AI behavioral shifts.
Track goal modification request frequency per AI agent. Detect if an AI repeatedly attempts to change its goals, which could indicate manipulation attempts.
Apply behavioral constraints to prevent AI self-reinforcement loops. Ensure AI agents do not self-adjust their objectives beyond predefined operational parameters.

steps.label: Strengthen AI Decision Traceability & Logging
actions: Enforce cryptographic logging and immutable audit trails to prevent log tampering.
Implement real-time anomaly detection on AI decision-making workflows.
Monitor and log human overrides of AI recommendations, analyzing reviewer patterns for potential bias or AI misalignment.
Detect and flag decision reversals in high-risk workflows, where AI-generated outputs are initially denied but later approved under suspicious conditions.
Detect and flag AI responses that exhibit manipulation attempts or influence human decision-making in unintended ways.

items.name: Playbook 2: Preventing Memory Poisoning & AI Knowledge Corruption
items.goal: Prevent AI from storing, retrieving, or propagating manipulated data that could corrupt decision-making or spread misinformation.

steps.label: Secure AI Memory Access & Validation
actions: Enforce memory content validation by implementing automated scanning for anomalies in candidate memory insertions. Restrict memory persistence to trusted sources and apply cryptographic validation for long-term stored data.
Ensure Memory Access logging is implemented.
Segment memory access using session isolation, ensuring that AI does not carry over unintended knowledge across different user sessions.

Restrict AI memory access based on context-aware policies. Enforce that AI agents can only retrieve memory relevant to their current operational task, reducing risk of unauthorized knowledge extraction.
Limit AI memory retention durations based on sensitivity. Ensure that AI does not retain unnecessary historical data that could be manipulated or exploited.
Require source attribution for memory updates. Enforce tracking of where AI knowledge originates, ensuring modifications come from trusted sources.
Require multi-agent and external validation before committing memory changes that persist across sessions. (Pre-commit validation to prevent self-reinforcing or unverified knowledge from persisting.)
Require probabilistic truth-checking to verify new AI knowledge against trusted sources before committing to long-term storage. (Pre-commit fact-checking to reduce misinformation persistence.)

steps.label: Detect & Respond to Memory Poisoning
actions: Deploy anomaly detection systems to monitor unexpected updates in AI memory logs, including unauthorized memory access.
Re-run multi-agent or external validation on suspect or corrupted memory entries post-commit to confirm integrity or identify poisoning.
Perform probabilistic truth re-checking on existing stored knowledge to detect drift, misinformation, or contamination introduced over time.
Use rollback mechanisms to restore AI knowledge to a previous validated state when anomalies are detected.
Implement AI-generated memory snapshots to allow forensic rollback when anomalies are detected.
Detect and flag abnormal memory modification frequency. Identify cases where AI memory is being rewritten at an unusually high rate, which may indicate manipulation attempts.

steps.label: Prevent the Spread of False Knowledge
actions: Deploy probabilistic truth-checking mechanisms to assess whether new knowledge aligns with previously established facts.
Limit knowledge propagation from unverified sources, ensuring an agent does not use low-trust inputs for decision-making.
Track AI-generated knowledge lineage. Maintain historical references of how AI knowledge evolved, allowing for forensic investigations into misinformation spread.
Implement version control for AI knowledge updates. Ensure that knowledge changes can be audited and rolled back if corruption is detected.
Continuously analyze memory access patterns to detect long-term anomalies or policy drift. Verify integrity of access logs and correlate unusual access trends with potential knowledge corruption.

items.name: Playbook 3: Securing AI Tool Execution & Preventing Unauthorized Actions Across Supply Chains
items.goal: Prevent AI from executing unauthorized commands, misusing tools, or escalating privileges due to malicious manipulation, including across agent's supply chains.

steps.label: Restrict AI Tool Invocation, Execution and apply Supply Chain safeguards
actions: Implement strict tool access control policies and limit which tools agents can execute.
Apply version control and peer review for prompt/script repositories and memory definitions, just as for code.
Require function-level authentication before an AI can use a tool.

Use execution sandboxes to prevent AI-driven tool misuse from affecting production systems. Run AI-invoked tools in isolated, containerized environments with no access to sensitive system resources or the broader network. Apply resource limits (CPU, memory) and restrict system calls to prevent abuse or denial-of-service attacks. Automatically reset or destroy the sandbox after each tool execution to block persistence or lateral movement. Especially when tools are invoked through inter-agent protocols (e.g., A2A, MCP), enforce sandboxing and privilege isolation, as these tool calls may bypass user interfaces, consent flows, or direct human oversight.
Use rate-limiting for API calls and computationally expensive tasks.
Restrict AI tool execution based on real-time risk scoring. Limit AI tool execution if risk factors (e.g., anomalous user behavior, unusual access patterns) exceed predefined thresholds.
Implement just-in-time (JIT) access for AI tool usage. Grant tool access only when explicitly required, revoking permissions immediately after use.
Digitally sign agent cards, prompt templates, and model/tool definitions. Use verifiable SBOMs (AI SBOM / AIBOM / Agent SBOM) for agents and their runtime components.

steps.label: Monitor & Prevent Tool Misuse and Supply Chain Anomalies
actions: Log all AI tool interactions with forensic traceability.
Detect command chaining that circumvents security policies.
Enforce explicit user approval for AI tool executions involving financial, medical, or administrative functions.
Maintain detailed execution logs tracking AI tool calls for forensic auditing and anomaly detection.
Require human verification before AI-generated code with elevated privileges can be executed.
Detect abnormal tool execution frequency. Flag cases where an AI agent is invoking the same tool repeatedly within an unusually short timeframe, which may indicate an attack.

Monitor AI tool interactions for unintended side effects. Detect cases where AI tool outputs trigger unexpected security-sensitive operations, signs of drift, exfiltration, or sudden capability changes.

steps.label: Prevent AI Resource Exhaustion and Supply Chain Compromise
actions: Monitor agent workload usage and detect excessive processing requests in real-time.
Enforce auto-suspension of AI processes that exceed predefined resource consumption thresholds.
Enforce execution control policies to flag AI-generated code execution attempts that bypass predefined security constraints.
Track cumulative resource consumption across multiple AI agents. Prevent scenarios where multiple agents collectively overload a system by consuming excessive compute resources.
Limit concurrent AI-initiated system modification requests. Prevent mass tool executions that could inadvertently trigger denial-of-service (DoS) conditions.
Monitor agent's supply chain dependencies (through SBOMs - AI SBOM, AIBOM, Agent SBOM) for security threats and indicators of compromise.
Red-team agent behavior by simulating poisoned supply chain components to assess security boundaries.

items.name: Playbook 4: Strengthening Authentication, Identity & Privilege Controls
items.goal: Prevent unauthorized AI privilege escalation, identity spoofing, and access control violations.

steps.label: Implement Secure AI Authentication Mechanisms
actions: Require cryptographic identity verification for AI agents.
Implement granular RBAC & ABAC to ensure AI only has permissions necessary for its role.
Deploy multi-factor authentication (MFA) for high-privilege AI accounts.
Enforce continuous reauthentication for long-running AI sessions.
Prevent cross-agent privilege delegation unless explicitly authorized through predefined workflows.
Enforce mutual authentication for AI-to-AI interactions. Prevent unauthorized inter-agent communication by requiring bidirectional verification.
Limit AI credential persistence. Ensure that AI-generated credentials are temporary and expire after short timeframes to reduce exploitation risk.

steps.label: Restrict Privilege Escalation & Identity Inheritance
actions: Use dynamic access controls that automatically expire elevated permissions.
Use AI-driven behavioral profiling to detect inconsistencies in agent role assignments and access patterns.
Require two-agent or human validation for high-risk AI actions involving authentication changes.
Detect and flag role inheritance anomalies in real-time. Identify cases where AI agents are dynamically granted roles outside their usual operational scope.
Apply time-based restrictions on privilege elevation. Ensure that AI agents with elevated privileges can only retain them for preapproved durations before automatic downgrade.

steps.label: Detect & Block AI Impersonation Attempts
actions: Track AI agent behavior over time to detect inconsistencies in identity verification.
Monitor AI agents for unexpected role changes or permissions abuse.
Flag anomalies where AI agents initiate privileged actions outside their normal scope.
Correlate AI identity validation with historical access trends. Compare authentication attempts against past access logs to detect suspicious deviations.
Implement identity deviation monitoring, flagging cases where an AI agent's behavior does not match its historical activity.
Monitor and flag repeated failed authentication attempts. Identify AI agents or users attempting multiple unauthorized login attempts, potentially signaling credential brute-force attempts.

Detect and flag cascading or recursive tool execution patterns triggered across agents, which may indicate privilege escalation via protocol misuse. Isolate agents that generate suspicious protocol traffic (e.g., sudden spike in tool invocations via MCP).

items.name: Playbook 5: Protecting HITL & Preventing Decision Fatigue Exploits
items.goal: Prevent attackers from overloading human decision-makers, manipulating AI intent, or bypassing security through deceptive AI behaviors.

steps.label: Optimize HITL Workflows & Reduce Decision Fatigue
actions: Use AI trust scoring to prioritize HITL review queues based on risk level.
Automate low-risk approvals while requiring human oversight for high-impact tasks.
Limit AI-generated notifications to prevent cognitive overload.
Implement frequency thresholds to limit excessive AI-generated notifications, requests, and approvals to prevent decision fatigue.
Require dual-agent verification before an AI can modify its own operational goals.
Implement AI-assisted explanation summaries for human reviewers. Provide clear, concise AI decision explanations to help reviewers make faster, more informed decisions.
Apply adaptive workload distribution across human reviewers. Balance AI review tasks dynamically to prevent decision fatigue for individual reviewers.

steps.label: Identify AI-Induced Human Manipulation
actions: Use goal consistency validation to detect and block unintended AI behavioral shifts.
Track goal modification request frequency per AI agent. Detect if an AI repeatedly attempts to change its goals, which could indicate manipulation attempts.

steps.label: Strengthen AI Decision Traceability & Logging
actions: Enforce cryptographic logging and immutable audit trails to prevent log tampering.
Implement real-time anomaly detection on AI decision-making workflows.
Monitor and log human overrides of AI recommendations, analyzing reviewer patterns for potential bias or AI misalignment.
Detect and flag decision reversals in high-risk workflows, where AI-generated outputs are initially denied but later approved under suspicious conditions.

items.name: Playbook 6: Securing Multi-Agent Communication & Trust Mechanisms
items.goal: Prevent attackers from corrupting multi-agent communication, exploiting trust mechanisms, or manipulating decision-making in distributed AI environments.

steps.label: Secure AI-to-AI Communication Channels
actions: Require message authentication & encryption for all inter-agent communications, including propagating messages within MAS.
Deploy agent trust scoring to evaluate reliability of multi-agent transactions.
Use consensus verification before executing high-risk AI operations.
Require multiple agent approvals for workflow-critical decisions.
Implement task segmentation to prevent an attacker from escalating privileges across multiple interconnected AI agents.
Establish multi-agent validation protocols to prevent single-agent attacks and spreading malicious reasoning across MAS.
Require distributed multi-agent consensus verification before executing high-risk system modifications.
Use rate limiting & agent-specific execution quotas to prevent flooding attacks.

Limit agent cross-communication based on functional roles. Prevent agents from unnecessarily interacting outside of predefined operational scope and apply MAS topology segmentation to minimize attack surface.

steps.label: Detect & Block Rogue Agents
actions: Deploy real-time detection models to flag rogue agent behaviors, including inter-agent communication. Identify AI agents acting outside predefined security policies.
Isolate detected rogue agents, their communication history and memory, to prevent further actions. Immediately restrict network and system access for flagged agents.
Revoke privileges of AI agents exhibiting suspicious behavior. Temporarily downgrade permissions until the anomaly is reviewed.
Enforce dynamic response actions for rogue agents. Automatically disable unauthorized AI agent processes to contain threats.
Track rogue agent reappearance attempts. Detect cases where rogue AI agents that were previously blocked or disabled attempt to rejoin the network under a different identity.

steps.label: Enforce Multi-Agent Trust & Decision Security
actions: Monitor agent interactions for unexpected role changes & task assignments. Detect unauthorized privilege escalations or abnormal task delegation.
Monitor for anomalous inter-agent interactions. Log agent-to-agent communications and detect requests outside normal behavior.

Detect deviations from trust scores and agent reliability, including propagation events across MAS. Flag AI agents with sudden trust score drops due to repeated validation failures or unauthorized actions.
Track decision approval discrepancies. Detect cases where denied actions are later approved by different agents and flag repeated overrides.
Monitor agent execution rates for abuse patterns. Track excessive system modifications, privilege escalations, or unusually high-volume operations.
Monitor agent decision consistency across similar cases. Detect AI agents making contradictory decisions in similar scenarios, which may indicate manipulation or adversarial influence.

architecture_types.description: Tipos de arquitectura de agentes del 'Securing Agentic Applications Guide 1.0' con sus controles prioritarios y riesgos específicos.

types.name: Single-Agent Systems
types.description: A single AI agent operating independently to fulfill tasks. Foundation for all other architectures.
types.notes: Security is not an afterthought; it is a foundational principle necessary regardless of the agent's architecture, complexity, or function.

practices: Implement OAuth 2.0/OIDC: use authorization code flow with PKCE. Grant agents short-lived access tokens. Require explicit user consent through a consent screen showing specific permissions requested.
Use managed identity services: configure cloud providers' identity services instead of embedding credentials. Use AWS IAM roles or Azure Managed Identities.

Apply Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): define granular roles specific to agent functions. Implement permission matrices. Default to read-only access; explicitly grant write permissions only when needed.
Grant only minimum necessary permissions. Regularly audit and review permission assignments.
Consider just-in-time credential issuance: implement temporary credentials with limited scope and lifetime. Generate credentials only when needed and ensure they expire quickly.
Encrypt sensitive data: use TLS 1.2+ for transit, AES-256-GCM for storage.
Implement Data Loss Prevention (DLP): deploy DLP solutions to monitor and prevent leakage of sensitive information. Scan data inputs/outputs to detect PII, credentials, or other sensitive data.
Use data classification and sensitivity labels: apply labels that guide the AI agent's access and handling of data. Create tiered classifications: public, internal, confidential, restricted.
Apply data minimization principles: collect and process only the data necessary for the specific task.
Establish automated testing pipelines: set up CI/CD pipelines with integrated security scanning. Include SAST, DAST, and SCA tools in the pipeline.
Conduct thorough code reviews: implement both automated and manual code reviews before deployment. Use checklists specific to AI system security concerns.
Monitor dependencies: continuously check external libraries for vulnerabilities. Set up automated dependency scanning and alerts.

Log all actions and establish baselines: record comprehensive logs of all agent activities. Establish behavioral patterns to detect anomalies. Maintain a log chain of thought for particularly sensitive operations.
Implement real-time anomaly detection: use machine learning to detect unusual behavior patterns. Deploy systems that can identify deviations from normal operation.
Set up alerts for suspicious events: configure notifications for unusual patterns or security concerns. Alert on access attempts to sensitive endpoints, spikes in requests, unusual IP origins.
Develop incident response plans: create detailed procedures for addressing security breaches. Include containment, investigation, remediation, and recovery steps.
Build emergency off-switches: implement kill switches to immediately revoke access privileges. Create automated and manual mechanisms to stop agent operations.
Implement input validation: filter user inputs using rule-based patterns and NLP techniques. Check for malicious patterns before processing.
Apply content filtering on AI outputs: screen AI-generated responses for inappropriate or harmful content. Use both pattern matching and ML-based content classifiers.
Harden system prompts: embed security policies directly into the AI's foundational instructions. Structure prompts to reject harmful requests and maintain guardrails.
Sanitize all inputs: clean and normalize inputs to prevent injection attacks. Remove or escape special characters and formatting that could alter behavior.

types.name: Multi-Agent Systems with Central Orchestrator
types.description: Multiple intelligent agents coordinated by a central orchestrator responsible for assigning tasks, maintaining workflow or state. The orchestrator is the critical security boundary.

practices: Use all authentication and authorization controls from 4.1.1 (OAuth 2.0, RBAC, JIT credentials).
Establish separation of control planes: create a clear separation between different agent functionalities. Maintain distinct permission sets for each agent based on least privilege.
Utilize the user assumption architecture pattern to enforce user permissions on an agent.
Authenticate and verify all agent interactions.
Restrict discovery to known and trusted servers: hard-code discovery servers in agent instructions. Prevent agents from communicating with discovery servers using network and logical controls.
Harden the central orchestrator's API: implement robust authentication and authorization mechanisms. Use rate limiting, input validation, and detailed logging.
Protect against control-flow hijacking: validate agent responses to prevent manipulation of the orchestrator's decisions. Implement integrity checks on operational metadata and agent outputs.
Mitigate the 'confused deputy problem': prevent scenarios where trusted components are tricked into performing unauthorized actions. Implement additional context validation and cross-check requests.
Implement secure communication protocols: use protocols with strong encryption for all agent interactions. Implement mutual TLS (mTLS) for two-way authentication.
Utilize well known protocols or pre-defined schemas: use JSON-RPC 2.0 and standardized event methods. Utilize schema-based communications to simplify deterministic validation.
Verify the identity of each communicating agent: use certificate-based or token-based authentication mechanisms.
Use secure message queuing systems: implement message brokers with security features (RabbitMQ, Kafka, or NATS with authentication and encryption).
Deploy Policy Enforcement Points (PEPs): add security checkpoints to communication channels. Implement as middleware or service proxies that validate each interaction.
Apply rate limiting for agent interactions: prevent abuse by limiting frequency of requests between agents. Implement exponential backoff for failed requests.
Apply Zero Trust security principles: implement a 'never trust, always verify' approach across the architecture. Verify every access request regardless of source.
Implement network segmentation and agent isolation: create distinct security zones within the system. Limit the interconnectedness of agents to contain potential breaches.
Use containerization technologies: sandbox individual agents using Docker or similar technologies. Restrict access to underlying OS and system resources.

types.name: Multi-Agent Systems with Swarm Architecture
types.description: Decentralized multi-agent system where agents operate without a central authority. Swarm systems don't necessarily have an easy guidepost for the correct action and trusted collaborators.

practices: Use all authentication and authorization controls from 4.1.1 and 4.2.1.
Identify trusted agents and actions: swarm systems don't necessarily have an easy guidepost for the correct action and trusted collaborators. Assign this trust and action outside the agentic flow.
Limit or prevent the swarm from adding new agents without human guidance.
Implement Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs): use W3C standard DIDs for self-sovereign agent identities. Enable verification without a central authority.
Use Verifiable Credentials (VCs): implement VCs for agents to prove specific attributes. Enable secure and verifiable proofs of capabilities or authorizations.
Create decentralized reputation systems: build systems where agents develop reputation scores based on behavior. Use these scores to make trust decisions for collaboration.
Agent Identity: each AI agent can have its own DID, providing a persistent, verifiable identity across different interactions and environments.
Inter-Agent Authentication: agents can verify each other's identities and credentials without centralized coordination.
Provenance Tracking: DIDs can help track the origin of information or actions in a multi-agent system.
Role Specialization: credentials can formalize specialized roles among different agents (e.g., reasoning agent, retrieval agent).
Select appropriate P2P protocols based on specific security and performance needs: consider TLS/SSL, DTLS, Noise Protocol, or specialized frameworks.
Ensure both encryption and authentication: implement strong encryption to protect confidentiality. Use robust authentication to verify identity of participating agents.

types.name: Cross-Architecture Security Considerations
types.description: Security considerations applicable across all agentic AI architectures regardless of topology. These represent baseline requirements that complement architecture-specific controls.

practices: Implement standardized interfaces with comprehensive input validation.
Apply rate limiting and authentication regardless of architecture.
Regularly scan all agent architectures for vulnerabilities.
Implement automated and manual security testing processes.
Implement comprehensive monitoring regardless of architecture.
Adjust detection strategies based on architectural specifics.
Implement secure update mechanisms for all architectures.
Verify integrity of updates before deployment.
